summary: Specifies the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol, the way hosts transfer electronic mail to each other. It was based on the earlier Mail Transfer Protocol work. Replaced by RFC 821.

eli5.summary: The rules that mail computers use to hand email to one another, like a polite conversation: who is it from, who is it for, here is the message.

subtitle: How mail computers hand email to each other reliably and efficiently.

tldr.problem: Email needs to be transmitted reliably from one host to another, and hosts on different networks need a standard protocol to relay mail through intermediate servers.
tldr.mechanism: SMTP is a command-response protocol where a sender connects to a receiver and sends MAIL (from), RCPT (to), and DATA commands in order. The receiver replies after each command. Mail can be relayed through multiple servers by moving addressing information between forward-paths and reverse-paths.
tldr.outcome: SMTP became the standard for mail transmission in the Internet. RFC 788 was later superseded by RFC 821 with minor updates, and SMTP remains in use today as the core mail delivery protocol.

today: RFC 788 was superseded by RFC 821, which makes minor clarifications and corrections. SMTP remains the standard protocol for mail transmission on the Internet and is used in every modern email system.

sections.title: The SMTP Goal and Model
sections.content: The objective of the Simple Mail Transfer Protocol (SMTP) is to transfer mail reliably and efficiently. SMTP works independent of the particular transport subsystem, requiring only a reliable ordered data stream channel. The protocol is based on a client-server model: a sender-SMTP establishes a connection to a receiver-SMTP, which may be the final destination or an intermediate relay host. The receiver-SMTP sends a greeting reply, and a lock-step dialog of commands and replies follows.
sections.eli5: SMTP is a set of rules for how computers talk when they send email: the sender speaks, the receiver listens and replies, one thing at a time.

sections.title: The Mail Transaction and Relay
sections.content:
A mail transaction has three steps. The sender issues a MAIL command with the reverse-path (who the mail is from), the receiver replies with OK. Then one or more RCPT commands specify recipients with forward-paths; each gets an OK or rejection. Finally, a DATA command starts mail data entry; the sender sends lines of text and ends with a line containing only a period. The receiver stores the message and replies OK.

SMTP also supports relaying: the forward-path can be a source route telling the mail where to go next. When a server relays mail, it moves its own identifier from the forward-path to the reverse-path, creating a return path for error notifications. If delivery fails, a bounce message is sent back to the address in the reverse-path.
sections.eli5: To send mail, you say who it is from, then who it is for, then send the message. If it is going to another host, you tell it where to go next. If something breaks, the receiver sends a message back to the sender saying what went wrong.

sections.title: Commands and Special Features
sections.content: The core commands are HELO (identify yourself), MAIL (start transaction), RCPT (name a recipient), DATA (send message), and QUIT (close connection). Additional commands include VRFY (verify a user name) and EXPN (expand a mailing list), which are optional and not required in the minimum implementation. The RFC also defines SEND, SOML, and SAML commands to deliver messages to users' terminals instead of or in addition to mailboxes. Reply codes are three-digit numbers: 250 means OK, 550 means failure. The mail data includes memo headers (From, To, Subject, Date) and is transparent—if a line in the text begins with a period, it is escaped so the end-of-data marker is unambiguous.
sections.eli5: SMTP has simple commands: MAIL, RCPT, and DATA do the main work. Other commands let you check names, expand lists, or send messages to screens. Three-digit reply codes tell you whether each step worked.
